title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 38
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Building for an Audience
passages.text:
A. The shape of a theatre determines what can be performed in it, and this constraint has been more decisive than any change in taste. An open-air arena where several thousand people sit on a hillside requires a performance projected outwards, in broad gesture and declaimed speech, with masks that carry a character to the back row. Intimacy is not a stylistic option in such a space; it is inaudible.

B. Roofing the building changed the writing. Enclosure permitted artificial light, which permitted control of when and where the audience could see, and it reduced the distances involved, which permitted speech at conversational volume and expression that depended on a face. The interior scenes, quiet exchanges and psychological detail that came to dominate drama followed the architecture rather than preceding it.

C. Lighting technology carried a hidden cost for a long period. Flame illumination meant that every performance took place in a building full of open fire surrounded by painted cloth, and the record of theatre fires through the era is correspondingly grim. Much of the regulation that still governs these buildings — exit widths, separating curtains, materials — dates from that period and from specific disasters.

D. The auditorium encoded a social arrangement as precisely as it did an acoustic one. Separate entrances, separate stairs and separately priced tiers meant that audiences of different means occupied the same building without meeting, and the sightlines from the cheapest seats were frequently poor because those seats existed to fill capacity rather than to serve their occupants. Reading a theatre plan tells you about a society.

E. Darkening the house was a change in the audience rather than in the stage. When the auditorium lights were lowered and kept low, attention was concentrated on the performance, conversation during the action became a breach rather than a norm, and the audience became a set of individuals facing one direction rather than a gathering that could see itself. The behaviour now considered proper is a recent invention with a technical cause.

F. The economics have always been difficult and have not become easier. A performance is made and consumed at the same moment, cannot be stored, and requires the same number of performers whether the house is full or half empty, so productivity gains available to almost every other industry are unavailable here. Costs rise with wages in the wider economy while output per performance cannot, which is why this sector everywhere depends on subsidy, patronage or a tolerance of low pay.

passages.title: Water from the Sea
passages.text:
Removing salt from seawater is not difficult and never has been; boiling it and condensing the steam works, and ships have done so for centuries. The whole subject is a question of energy per unit of water, because the process has a theoretical minimum energy requirement set by physics, and every practical method uses several times that minimum. Desalination is therefore best understood as a way of converting energy into water at a known and improving rate.

The dominant method now is not distillation but filtration under pressure. Forcing seawater against a membrane that passes water and rejects dissolved salts requires pressure rather than heat, and the energy needed has fallen substantially — largely through recovering pressure from the outgoing brine stream and reusing it, which is an engineering refinement rather than a new principle. Costs fell by a large factor over several decades and the decline has slowed as the process approaches its physical limits.

The waste stream is the constraint most often omitted from discussion. What leaves the plant is roughly half the intake volume at roughly twice the salinity, warmer than the sea and containing the chemicals used to keep the membranes clean. Discharged carelessly into a shallow or enclosed bay, it settles and damages the sea floor community; discharged through a properly designed diffuser into moving water, it disperses to background levels within a modest distance. The difference is engineering and enforcement rather than an inherent property of the process.

Where desalination makes sense is narrower than its advocates suggest and wider than its critics allow. For a coastal city with reliable electricity and no cheaper source, it is a sound answer that removes dependence on rainfall entirely. For agriculture it is almost never viable, because crops need water in quantities whose value per unit is far below what desalinated water costs, and proposals to irrigate deserts with it founder on that arithmetic rather than on any technical obstacle.

The comparison that matters is with the alternatives rather than with nothing. Reducing losses from distribution networks, which run at a quarter or more of supply in many cities, treating and reusing wastewater, and pricing water so that its use reflects its scarcity are all cheaper per unit of water made available than building a plant. Desalination competes with these options and is frequently chosen over them because it is a visible project with a ribbon to cut rather than a decade of unglamorous maintenance.

The strategic argument for it is nonetheless real and separate from the cost comparison. A plant provides supply that does not depend on the weather, which is worth something in itself as climate variability increases, and that value is a form of insurance rather than an operating saving. Insurance is worth buying and is worth buying knowingly, at a price compared against other ways of achieving the same security.

passages.title: Permission to Work
passages.text:
A licence to practise a trade is defended on grounds of consumer protection and functions, in a substantial number of cases, as a restriction on entry. Both statements are true, and the proportions differ so much between occupations that arguing about licensing in general produces no useful conclusion. The question worth asking is always about a particular licence: what harm does it prevent, and what does it cost the people it excludes?

Where the case is strong it is very strong. In occupations where an error is irreversible, where the customer cannot assess competence before purchase, and where the consequences fall on people other than the purchaser, a requirement to demonstrate training before practising is straightforwardly justified — surgery, aviation, electrical installation and structural engineering are not contested examples.

The growth in licensing has not been concentrated in those occupations. The share of the workforce requiring a licence has risen several-fold over recent decades in a number of countries, and much of the growth is in occupations where the potential harm is modest and recoverable. Where hairdressing, interior decoration or florist work requires hundreds of hours of instruction, the training requirement is doing something other than protecting the public from serious injury.

The evidence on outcomes is where the argument is settled less comfortably than either side expects. Studies generally find that licensing raises practitioners' earnings, raises prices for consumers, and reduces the number of people working in the occupation; they generally do not find corresponding improvements in measured quality, though quality is hard to measure and the absence of a finding is weaker than a finding of absence. What is consistently found is the price effect.

The distributional consequences fall on identifiable people. Fees and unpaid training hours are a barrier that is heaviest for those with the least capital, and licences that do not transfer between jurisdictions penalise anyone who moves — a particular problem for migrants whose qualifications are not recognised, and for military families and others who relocate frequently. The cost is concentrated on people entering, and the benefit on people already inside.

Better instruments exist for most of the middle ground. Certification that is voluntary conveys the same information to consumers who want it without excluding anyone; registration records who is practising without requiring permission to start; inspection targets the conduct rather than the entry. These serve the informational purpose that licensing is defended for, and they are less attractive to existing practitioners for exactly the reason that they do not limit competition.
